body:
Give credit to the original source

Source attribution means identifying where information, words, ideas, pictures or other material came from. It helps readers trace a statement to its origin and recognises the creator's contribution. In a school project, a useful attribution identifies the author or organisation, the work or page and enough detail to locate it. When quoting exact words, distinguish the quotation from your own explanation; when paraphrasing someone else's idea, still acknowledge its source.

Plagiarism means presenting another person's work or idea as though it were your own. Changing a few words without acknowledging the original source can still be plagiarism. Giving credit is an important academic and ethical duty, even when a source is freely accessible.

Attribution and permission answer different questions

ConceptQuestion it answersExample
AttributionWho created the material or supplied the information?Name the author and publication used in an explanation
Permission or licenceIs this use of the material allowed?Check whether a photograph may be republished
VerificationIs the factual claim reliable?Compare a claim with the original notice or trustworthy evidence

Copyright protects qualifying original works, such as writing, photographs, recordings and software. Copyright infringement involves use that violates the rights of the copyright holder. Attribution alone does not automatically authorise reproduction of an entire protected image or article. Reuse may be allowed under a suitable licence, permission or applicable legal exception; what is allowed depends on the work, use and relevant rules. By contrast, plagiarism focuses on falsely claiming authorship or ownership of an idea or work. The 2 problems can overlap but are not identical.

A responsible way to reuse online material

Trace a quotation or image to its creator rather than relying only on the person who forwarded it. Identify the original title and context, check the terms of reuse, and provide suitable credit when using it. If the right to republish is unclear, use an original explanation or an appropriately licensed alternative instead of assuming that anything on the Internet is free to copy.

A student credits the photographer of an online image but copies it into a public advertisement without checking its licence. The credit identifies the creator, yet it does not by itself settle whether that reproduction is permitted.

Prelims focus

  • Attribution identifies the source of borrowed words, ideas or media.
  • Plagiarism presents another's contribution as one's own.
  • Copyright infringement concerns violation of copyright rights.
  • Verification tests truth; a citation alone does not prove a claim is correct.
  • Trap: Naming an image's author does not automatically grant permission to republish it.

[NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Ch. 11 'Societal Impact', §§11.4.1–11.4.3 'Intellectual Property Right', 'Violation of IPR' and 'Public Access and Open Source Software', pp. 235–238, 2026–27 reprint; CBSE, Digital Citizenship: Level 1 Student Handbook, Grade 6, Lesson 13 'What is Plagiarism and How to Avoid It', consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Identify the original source, check reuse rights and give credit; verify truth separately. Attribution alone does not grant reuse rights.
pictures.caption: Crediting a source and checking reuse rights are separate checks.

title: Source Attribution, Plagiarism and Permission to Reuse

body:
When information misleads

Digital media allows a false or incomplete statement to spread quickly, especially when people forward it because it appears urgent, surprising or important. Misinformation is false information shared without an intention to deceive. Disinformation is false or misleading information deliberately spread to deceive. The distinction usually concerns intent, which may not be obvious to an ordinary reader.

A person deliberately invents a false examination postponement notice: this is disinformation. Another person believes the notice and forwards it without checking: that forward is misinformation. The same false claim can spread through both behaviours.

Misleading content need not be entirely fabricated. An old but genuine notice may be circulated as if it were current; a photograph may be used with an incorrect place or date; or a true statistic may be quoted without an essential qualification. An opinion expresses a judgement and is not automatically a false factual claim. A fact is something established as true by evidence. Even a generally reputable source can make a mistake, and a message's popularity does not establish its accuracy.

Verify before forwarding

The most useful habit is to pause before passing on a claim whose truth matters. Examine the original source, the date, the context and whether an independent reliable source confirms it. A cropped screenshot without its complete notice or identifiable origin is weaker evidence than the original official announcement.

  1. Identify the exact claim. Separate a factual assertion from opinion, prediction or humour.
  2. Find its origin. Look for an author, issuing body, publication date and the complete original document.
  3. Cross-check. Compare with the responsible institution or other credible, independent evidence.
  4. Check the context. Confirm that dates, images and qualifications have not been removed or changed.
  5. Decide whether to share. Pass it on only when adequately supported, with the relevant source and context; otherwise refrain.

A Gujarat examination example

Suppose a messaging group circulates a picture saying that the Gujarat Public Service Commission has changed an examination date. A careful reader should look for the original notice on the Commission's official channels and compare the advertisement number and date. The Press Information Bureau (PIB) Fact Check Unit is an Indian example of an official fact-checking service, but its remit concerns claims related to the Government of India. It should not be assumed to verify every state-government or GPSC notification. PIB's official guidance, available at the 5 November 2026 content cutoff, states that the Unit began operations in November 2019 and confines its fact-check complaints to Union Government matters.

How to handle a mistake after sharing

If a claim you forwarded turns out to be false, correct it clearly in the same conversation or group where possible, explain what was inaccurate, and provide the verified source. Deleting the original message may help limit further spread but does not replace a correction because recipients may already have believed or copied it. Avoid repeating sensational false allegations unnecessarily when correcting them.

Balanced reporting and truthfulness are related but different. A report can contain accurate facts yet omit an important perspective; it can also fairly represent several opinions while getting a central fact wrong. Responsible reading examines both evidence and what relevant information may be missing.

Prelims focus

  • Misinformation: false information shared without deliberate deception.
  • Disinformation: deliberate spread of false or misleading information to deceive.
  • Check the original source, date, supporting evidence and context before forwarding.
  • PIB Fact Check Unit: operational from November 2019; concerned with Union Government-related claims.
  • For a GPSC claim, check the Commission's original notice rather than a forwarded screenshot.
  • Trap: A genuine old notice is not necessarily valid for a current examination.

[UNESCO, 'Misinformation' and 'Disinformation', UNESCO terminology entries, consulted 5 November 2026; UNESCO, 'Do you trust what you watch or read?', section 'The importance of media and information literacy', updated 20 April 2023; NCERT, Social and Political Life II, Class 7, Ch. 6 'Understanding Media', pp. 73–78, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, §11.3.3 'Social Media Etiquettes', p. 234, 2026–27 reprint; Press Information Bureau, 'Fact Check Unit: Frequently Asked Questions', questions 1, 2 and 4, consulted 5 November 2026; National Portal of India, 'Website of Gujarat Public Service Commission', consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Check a claim’s original issuer, date, evidence and context, then share with its source only if supported; correct any inaccurate earlier sharing.
pictures.caption: Check origin, date, evidence and context before forwarding a claim.

title: Misinformation, Verification and Responsible Forwarding

body:
What digital wellbeing involves

Digital wellbeing is the healthy and purposeful use of technology without allowing it to needlessly disrupt sleep, physical activity, concentration, relationships or daily responsibilities. Digital devices are useful for learning, communication and services; the goal is balanced use, not the complete avoidance of screens.

Long periods of uninterrupted screen use may contribute to discomfort, reduced movement or difficulties with attention and sleep. Constant notifications and distressing online content can also add stress for some people. The effects depend on what a person does online, their circumstances and whether use displaces necessary activities. Screen time alone does not establish an addiction or a mental-health condition.

Habits that protect attention and health

  • Set a purpose: open an app to complete a defined task instead of automatically browsing every notification.
  • Take breaks: rest the eyes, change posture and move regularly during prolonged study or work.
  • Protect sleep: reduce unnecessary device use before bedtime and keep a consistent sleep routine.
  • Manage interruptions: silence non-essential alerts during study, meetings or rest.
  • Keep offline balance: make time for physical activity, family, friends and interests beyond screens.
  • Respond to distress: step away from abusive or upsetting online content, use blocking or reporting options and seek support when needed.

There is no single screen-time number in this lesson that fits every age, activity and circumstance. Whether digital use is affecting health, sleep, study or relationships is a more useful first check than treating all screen time as equally harmful.

Apply the right question to each online action

A responsible netizen checks not only how a message is written, but also what is shared, whose interests are affected, where the information came from and whether the activity remains healthy. Respect, consent, privacy, attribution, verification and balance work together. The applicable question changes with the situation: a public comment needs civility; someone else's photograph needs consent; a copied passage needs attribution and legitimate reuse; and a startling news claim needs verification.

Prelims focus

  • Digital wellbeing means healthy, balanced and purposeful technology use.
  • Sleep, physical movement, concentration and offline relationships are relevant to digital habits.
  • Screen time measures use; it is not by itself a diagnosis of harmful dependence.
  • Reporting or blocking abuse can protect wellbeing without requiring a public argument.
  • Trap: Responsible digital conduct does not mean avoiding the Internet altogether.

[CBSE and Cyber Peace Foundation, Cyber Safety, 2020, Ch. 6 'Digital Health and Wellness', pp. 42–47; CBSE, Digital Citizenship: Level 1 Student Handbook, Grade 6, Lessons 9–10 'Importance of Tracking Your Screen Time' and 'Understanding How to Create Balance', consulted 5 November 2026; World Health Organization, 'Stress', section 'Sleep' and guidance on news exposure, consulted 5 November 2026; World Health Organization, 'Digital Environments and Mental Health', overview, consulted 5 November 2026.]
